cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Song Zhong lineage (clones of the old Wudong mother trees)
processing: Classic Wudong dancong processing: sun-withering, overnight shaking to a medium-light oxidation, strip rolling and a careful light-to-medium charcoal roast in several passes, with long rests between roasts.
harvest_season: One spring picking, late April to early May on Wudong; old trees are picked by hand over a few days and processed in small separate batches.
appearance_dry: Long, heavy, dark brown strips with a slight sheen and a deep honeyed, woody smell.
appearance_liquor: Deep gold to orange-amber, clear and oily-looking.
appearance_wet: Large, thick, leathery olive leaves with red edges, slow to open.
taste_profile: Dense and layered: honey, dried fruit and a gardenia or orchid aroma depending on the lineage, a thick body, a woody old-tree depth and a mineral, cooling aftertaste that Chaozhou drinkers call mountain rhyme (shan yun).

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps and full decanting. Use soft water. The character is in the texture and the aftertaste, so taste slowly and do not drink it after a perfumed tea.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, often with the tree or garden named; genuine old-tree lots are released in autumn after two or three roasts and rests, and are frequently sold a year or more after harvest once the fire has settled. They keep three to five years sealed and dry and are among the few dancongs that are deliberately aged, with the year stated.
description:
Song Zhong, Song-dynasty stock, is the name Chaozhou gives to the oldest lineage of Phoenix dancong: tea from the ancient mother trees on Wudong and from the cuttings taken from them. The claim in the name is that the line goes back to the Song dynasty; what is verifiable is that the surviving mother trees are several centuries old and that their descendants make the deepest, most expensive dancong there is.

The most famous tree stands at Li Zai Ping on Wudong at over a thousand metres, a gardenia-type (Huang Zhi Xiang) dancong that locals date to the Song and that has been photographed by every visitor to the mountain. Song Zhong is therefore not one aroma: you will meet Song Zhong Huang Zhi Xiang, Song Zhong Mi Lan Xiang, Song Zhong Dong Fang Hong and others, each a clone or seedling line traced to an old tree. What they share is age, altitude and the old-tree character.

The making is the classic Wudong method, with the oxidation kept medium-light and the charcoal roast light to medium, done in several passes over the summer with weeks of rest between them. Old-tree leaf is thick and tolerates that patient roasting, which is where the dried-fruit and woody notes come from.

In the cup the aroma is quieter than a Ya Shi Xiang and the body is far thicker: honey, dried longan, gardenia or orchid, a resinous woodiness, and the long, cool, mineral aftertaste called shan yun that is the whole reason for the price. It runs ten steeps and more and is best in the middle and end of the session; brew it with boiling water, flash steeps, soft water, and never straight after a perfumed tea.

Buying is a trust exercise. Real old-tree Song Zhong is made in kilograms, not tonnes, and the name is used freely for ordinary Wudong and even for lowland tea. Buy from a seller who names the garden or the tree and the year, start with a small sample, and compare it with a good high-mountain Huang Zhi Xiang: if the Song Zhong is not clearly deeper and longer, the label is doing the work.
sources_note: The Song-dynasty dating is traditional; the Li Zai Ping mother tree is usually described as roughly 600 years old and of the Huang Zhi Xiang type. Reports about the health or death of individual mother trees vary and are not stated here.
